papers.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
papers.abstract: As available training data approaches its physical limit, gains from Scaling Laws have begun to diminish. Consequently, improving Large Language Models (LLMs) now depends less on data expansion and more on higher-quality data utilization. However, in the context of large-scale corpora, existing refinement methodologies face significant limitations in quality, efficiency, and reliability: Rule-based approaches are constrained by fixed heuristics and struggle with instance-level variations; LLM-based approaches improve quality but fail to meet the efficiency and reliability requirements of large-scale data processing. To address these challenges, we propose UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework for large-scale pre-training data that completes the editing function space by introducing insertion in addition to deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level editing. Specifically, UltraX builds a reliable program-supervision generation pipeline. In this pipeline, dataset-adaptive prompt optimization first guides an expert LLM to produce high-quality end-to-end refined texts, and Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement then convert original-refined text pairs into structured program supervision. Meanwhile, UltraX improves supervision quality and stabilizes the training distribution with low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination. During inference and execution, it normalizes and validates model outputs through sliding-window prediction, global operation aggregation, and systematic post-processing, improving the stability and reliability of large-scale execution. Experiments show that UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all corpora and also matches or surpasses baselines with fewer training tokens, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability.

summary.takeaway: UltraX introduces a function-calling refinement framework with insertion, deletion, and modification operations, achieving superior data refinement quality and efficiency for large-scale LLM pre-training.
summary.problem: Existing large-scale pre-training data refinement methods either lack fine-grained editing capabilities or fail to scale efficiently and reliably to massive corpora.
summary.method: UltraX constructs a program-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, dynamic context replacement, and robust execution with sliding-window prediction and post-processing.
summary.evidence: Experiments with 1B parameter models pretrained on multiple corpora show UltraX surpasses baselines by over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets while using fewer training tokens.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UltraX’s performance on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation nor does it address potential biases inherited from expert LLMs used in supervision generation.
summary.why_for_you: UltraX offers a scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement approach that improves pre-training data quality and efficiency, directly addressing challenges in trustworthy and efficient LLM data utilization.

signals.text: UltraX achieves over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets in downstream tasks using 1B parameter models pretrained from scratch, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability compared to baselines.

UltraX’s program-supervision pipeline includes dataset-adaptive prompt optimization guiding an expert LLM to generate high-quality refined texts, followed by line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement to convert text pairs into structured editing programs.

UltraX stabilizes training distribution and improves supervision quality via low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination, while inference uses sliding-window prediction and global operation aggregation to ensure stable large-scale execution.

deep_dive.overview: UltraX addresses the diminishing returns of scaling LLM training data by focusing on improving data quality through fine-grained, programmatic editing of pre-training corpora. Unlike prior rule-based or LLM-based refinement methods limited by fixed heuristics or computational inefficiency, UltraX completes the editing function space by adding insertion to deletion and modification, enabling nuanced instance-level edits. It constructs a reliable program supervision pipeline where an expert LLM, guided by dataset-adaptive prompts, produces end-to-end refined texts. These are converted into structured editing operations via line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement. To ensure training stability and quality, UltraX filters low-confidence examples and controls sampling ratios of operation types. During inference, it segments long documents with sliding windows, predicts local operations, aggregates them globally, and applies systematic post-processing to produce stable, executable refinement programs. Experiments with 1B models pretrained on multiple corpora demonstrate UltraX’s superior average performance and data efficiency, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on several datasets, validating its approach to scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement for LLM pre-training.

methodology.title: Dataset-Adaptive Prompt Optimization
methodology.detail: UltraX first optimizes prompts tailored to each dataset to guide an expert LLM in generating high-quality, end-to-end refined texts from raw inputs, ensuring that the refinement captures dataset-specific nuances and semantic improvements.

methodology.title: Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement
methodology.detail: These techniques convert original and refined text pairs into structured program supervision by aligning lines between versions and replacing context dynamically, enabling the extraction of precise editing operations such as insertion, deletion, and modification.

methodology.title: Low-Confidence Example Filtering and Ratio-Controlled Sampling
methodology.detail: To improve supervision quality and stabilize training, UltraX filters out examples with low confidence scores and controls the sampling ratio of different operation combinations, balancing the training distribution across insertion, deletion, and modification operations.

methodology.title: Sliding-Window Segment-wise Operation Prediction
methodology.detail: During inference, UltraX segments long documents using a sliding-window approach, normalizes line numbers, and independently predicts editing operation sequences for each segment to handle length constraints and maintain local context.

methodology.title: Global Operation Aggregation and Systematic Post-Processing
methodology.detail: Local operation sequences from segments are merged into a global program by mapping operations to global line numbers, filtering duplicates, merging adjacent or interfering operations, and applying fallback mechanisms to ensure stable, executable refinement programs.

mechanism.title: Programmatic Editing with Complete Operation Space
mechanism.detail: UltraX extends the editing function space by including insertion alongside deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level edits that preserve semantic coherence and restore missing information, overcoming limitations of prior deletion-only or replacement-only frameworks.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes a deterministic function executor that applies predicted editing operations to original texts, ensuring auditable and interpretable refinement.

experiments.title: Pretraining 1B Parameter Models on Multiple Corpora
experiments.detail: UltraX was evaluated by pretraining 1B parameter language models from scratch on multiple large-scale corpora, comparing downstream task performance against baselines including raw data and ProX refinement, measuring average accuracy improvements and data efficiency.

experiments.title: Downstream Task Evaluation Across Ten Tasks
experiments.detail: Performance was assessed on ten downstream tasks including ARC-C, ARC-E, CSQA, HellaS, MMLU, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoG, and SciQ, with varying numbers of training tokens, demonstrating consistent gains and surpassing baselines with fewer tokens.

experiments.title: Ablation on Operation Combination Sampling
experiments.detail: The effect of ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination was analyzed to understand its impact on training stability and refinement quality, showing that balanced sampling improves model performance.

findings.title: Superior Average Performance
findings.detail: UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all evaluated corpora, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on multiple datasets compared to baseline methods.

findings.title: Improved Data Efficiency
findings.detail: UltraX matches or surpasses baseline refinement methods while using fewer training tokens, indicating stronger data efficiency in pre-training.

findings.title: Fine-Grained Refinement Balances Noise Removal and Preservation
findings.detail: Analyses suggest UltraX’s inclusion of insertion operations alongside deletion and modification enables better balance between removing noise and preserving useful information, reducing semantic fragmentation.

findings.title: Stable Large-Scale Execution
findings.detail: The sliding-window prediction, global aggregation, and systematic post-processing pipeline improve the stability and reliability of large-scale data refinement execution.

contributions: Proposed UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework introducing insertion to complete the editing function space for fine-grained instance-level editing.
Developed a reliable seed-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, and dynamic context replacement to generate structured program supervision.
Designed a robust large-scale execution pipeline with systematic post-processing to handle duplicate matching, ambiguous replacements, and operation interference.
Demonstrated consistent downstream performance improvements and stronger data efficiency across multiple large-scale pre-training corpora.
limitations: Lack of detailed evaluation on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation and its impact on refinement quality.
Potential biases and errors inherited from expert LLMs used in generating seed supervision are not explicitly analyzed.
No formal theoretical or causal mechanism is provided to explain the editing operation interactions or their effect on model performance.
Limited discussion on the computational cost and scalability trade-offs compared to other LLM-based refinement methods.
open_questions: How does UltraX perform on extremely long documents or streaming data beyond the sliding-window segmentation approach?
What are the effects of expert LLM biases on the quality and reliability of generated program supervision?
Can the programmatic editing framework be extended to incorporate semantic or syntactic constraints to further improve refinement quality?
How does UltraX compare in computational efficiency and cost to other state-of-the-art LLM-based refinement methods at larger model scales?

papers.title: Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier? Benchmarking Rubric LLMs for Deep-Research Source Attribution
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning increasingly relies on an LLM judge to score each rubric criterion, and that judge acts as the reward model during training. Before such a signal can be trusted, we need to know how capable the judge must be and how biased it is. We study this calibration question for citation quality in deep-research systems, where a search-grounded LLM must support each claim it writes with a cited source. Citation quality is a structured rubric task in which each attribution-citation pair is judged along two dimensions that require an LLM, source relevance and factual support. On an adversarial long-form benchmark, we score 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families against gold labels over 1,248 rubric decisions, all of which were human-reviewed and 378 of which were hard cases adjudicated from judge disagreements. Cheaper judges remain competitive across both dimensions, with GPT-5-mini attaining the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 ($κ$=0.636), while on factual support the judges are statistically indistinguishable (overlapping confidence intervals), so no single model dominates. At comparable F1, the judges still differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Scalar F1 obscures this directional bias, yet it is exactly what a downstream reinforcement learning loop would reinforce. Calibrating the judge is therefore a prerequisite for using citation rubrics as reward signals, and our results show that this calibration does not require the most expensive available model.

summary.takeaway: Cheaper off-the-shelf LLM judges can reliably evaluate citation quality for source relevance and factual support without requiring the most expensive frontier models.
summary.problem: Determining how capable and unbiased an LLM judge must be to serve as a trustworthy reward model for citation quality in deep-research systems.
summary.method: Benchmarking 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families on an adversarial long-form citation quality task with human-reviewed gold labels across source relevance and factual support dimensions.
summary.evidence: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 (κ=0.636), and judges were statistically indistinguishable on factual support, with detailed bias metrics revealing differences in pass-rate drift, false positive, and false negative rates.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide evidence on how judge calibration impacts downstream reinforcement learning training quality or explore mechanisms to correct directional biases in judges.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding judge calibration and bias in citation verification enables efficient and trustworthy reward modeling for RL training in deep-research LLM applications.

signals.text: GPT-5-mini attained the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 with Cohen’s κ=0.636, outperforming more expensive models on this dimension.
The evaluation framework uses a rubric with two LLM-judged criteria—source relevance and factual support—each scored binarily with rationale, enabling structured and interpretable judge assessments.

Despite comparable F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, indicating that scalar F1 metrics obscure directional biases critical for reinforcement learning reward signals.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the calibration of LLM judges used as reward models in reinforcement learning for citation quality in deep-research systems. The authors construct an adversarial benchmark spanning 25 diverse topics with 1,248 human-reviewed rubric decisions on source relevance and factual support. They evaluate 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families, measuring pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, and bias metrics such as pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Results show that smaller, cheaper models like GPT-5-mini can match or exceed the performance of larger frontier models on source relevance, while factual support judgments are statistically indistinguishable across judges. However, differences in directional bias metrics reveal that scalar accuracy metrics alone are insufficient to characterize judge reliability for downstream RL training. The study concludes that careful calibration of judges is essential but does not require the most expensive models, enabling more cost-effective and trustworthy citation verification in RL pipelines.

methodology.title: Benchmark Construction
methodology.detail: The Deep-Research Citation Benchmark includes 25 diverse topics with long-form summaries and adversarially edited claims using 19 strategies. Attribution-citation pairs are parsed and scored on three criteria: link accessibility (deterministic), source relevance, and factual support (both LLM-judged). A council of 6 LLM judges independently labels pairs, with human review validating all 1,248 decisions and adjudicating 378 hard cases.

methodology.title: Judge Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Judges produce binary pass/fail scores per criterion with free-text rationales. Metrics include pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ for agreement, pass-rate drift (judge vs. gold pass rate), false positive rate (accepting bad citations), and false negative rate (rejecting good citations). These metrics characterize both accuracy and directional bias relevant for RL reward signals.

methodology.title: Judge Models and Setup
methodology.detail: Eight LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families are evaluated via cloud inference APIs. Each judge scores all 624 source relevance and 624 factual support pairs. Two judges (GPT-5-mini and Claude Opus 4.6) also contributed to gold labels, enabling council-independent comparisons.

methodology.title: Prompt Design
methodology.detail: Prompts instruct judges to provide binary scores and rationales for source relevance and factual support, emphasizing expert evaluation criteria such as topical relevance, claim support, factual consistency, and contradiction detection. The same prompts are applied uniformly across all judges.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models explaining judge behavior or bias mechanisms, focusing instead on empirical benchmarking and metric analysis.

experiments.title: Adversarial Long-Form Citation Benchmark
experiments.detail: The benchmark contains 1,248 rubric decisions over 624 attribution-citation pairs, with 378 hard cases adjudicated by humans. Judges are evaluated on source relevance and factual support dimensions using pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate.

experiments.title: Judge Cost-Quality Tradeoff Analysis
experiments.detail: The study compares judge accuracy metrics against estimated cost per decision on a logarithmic scale, showing that cheaper judges like GPT-5-mini achieve competitive or superior performance relative to more expensive models.

findings.title: Cheaper Judges Competitive on Source Relevance
findings.detail: GPT-5-mini achieves the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 and Cohen’s κ of 0.636, outperforming larger models, demonstrating that smaller judges can reliably assess topical relevance.

findings.title: No Single Judge Dominates Factual Support
findings.detail: On factual support, judges’ performance overlaps within confidence intervals, indicating no statistically significant difference in accuracy among the evaluated models.

findings.title: Directional Biases Vary Across Judges
findings.detail: Despite similar F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, revealing biases that scalar metrics like F1 fail to capture but that affect RL reward signals.

contributions: Introduces a large adversarial benchmark for citation quality evaluation with human-reviewed gold labels across diverse topics.
Comprehensively evaluates 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges on source relevance and factual support, including bias metrics critical for RL reward modeling.
Demonstrates that smaller, cheaper LLM judges can match or exceed frontier models in citation verification tasks.
Highlights the importance of calibrating judges to account for directional biases that scalar accuracy metrics obscure.
limitations: Does not analyze the impact of judge calibration on downstream reinforcement learning training outcomes.
Lacks exploration of methods to mitigate or correct directional biases in judge models.
No mechanistic or theoretical explanation is provided for observed judge biases or performance differences.
Evaluation is limited to off-the-shelf models accessed via APIs, without fine-tuning or adaptation experiments.
open_questions: How do directional biases in LLM judges affect the stability and quality of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards?
What calibration or debiasing techniques can effectively reduce false positive and false negative rates in LLM judges?
Can smaller LLM judges be fine-tuned or adapted to further close gaps in factual support evaluation?
How does retrieval quality interact with judge performance and bias in citation verification pipelines?

papers.title: When the Judge Changes, So Does the Measurement: Auditing LLM-as-Judge Reliability
papers.abstract: An LLM-as-judge score can move even when the candidate responses stay fixed, simply because the evaluator has changed. We treat this evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem. Across four judgment datasets, we compare two upgrade paths available in practice: scaling Qwen3 dense judges from 1.7B to 32B parameters and moving across MiniMax M2-M2.7 released APIs. The main pattern is that judge upgrades are not interchangeable: only Qwen3 1.7B to 4B gives a robust adjacent gain, while MiniMax adjacent releases do not. Stronger judges reduce but do not remove position and verbosity bias. Repeated-sample juries add little when errors are correlated. Structured debate can move decisions substantially, but without parser and fallback logs those shifts cannot be attributed to deliberation. We argue that LLM-as-judge reports should include dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.

summary.takeaway: LLM-as-judge reliability varies with evaluator changes, showing that judge upgrades are not interchangeable and that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases or correlated errors.
summary.problem: Replacing an LLM evaluator changes measured scores even with fixed candidate responses, creating evaluator-replacement ambiguity that challenges measurement validity.
summary.method: The study compares two evaluator upgrade paths—Qwen3 parameter scaling (1.7B to 32B) and MiniMax M2–M2.7 API releases—across four judgment datasets, analyzing accuracy, bias, error correlation, and protocol auditability.
summary.evidence: Empirical results show only Qwen3 1.7B→4B scaling yields robust adjacent gains, MiniMax releases lack consistent gains, stronger judges reduce position and verbosity bias but do not remove them, and jury aggregation gains are limited by high error correlation.
summary.limitations: The study does not establish causal claims about MiniMax internals and lacks parser and fallback logs to fully attribute debate-induced decision shifts.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding evaluator-replacement ambiguity and multi-dimensional reliability components is critical for trustworthy LLM evaluation and designing robust LLM-as-judge protocols.

signals.text: Only the Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters produces a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability, while MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not yield consistent improvements across datasets.

The study operationalizes LLM-as-judge reliability into four components—judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability—measured via accuracy, Cohen’s κ, position flip rates, error correlation ρ, and parse status.
High intra-class error correlations (ρ up to 0.972 for Qwen3 juries) limit jury aggregation gains, as majority voting fails to amplify reliability when errors are dependent rather than independent.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the evaluator-replacement ambiguity in LLM-as-judge evaluation, where changing the evaluator model alters measured scores despite fixed candidate responses. It investigates whether improvements in judge reliability arise from increased evaluator capability or other factors like bias and protocol design. The authors compare two upgrade paths: parameter scaling of Qwen3 judges (1.7B to 32B parameters) and released-model upgrades of MiniMax M2 to M2.7 APIs, across four diverse judgment datasets. They decompose reliability into four operational components—accuracy, bias robustness, error correlation, and auditability—and analyze how these interact with evaluator scaling and aggregation protocols. Results show that only Qwen3 scaling from 1.7B to 4B yields robust gains, while MiniMax upgrades do not consistently improve reliability. Stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate position and verbosity biases. Jury aggregation gains are limited by high correlated errors, and debate protocols require audit trails to attribute decision shifts properly. The study advocates for comprehensive reporting standards including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol logs to improve measurement validity in LLM-as-judge evaluations.

methodology.title: Evaluator Upgrade Comparison
methodology.detail: Two evaluator upgrade paths are compared: Qwen3 dense judges scaled from 1.7B to 32B parameters, and MiniMax M2 to M2.7 released APIs. This comparison isolates parameter scaling effects from released-model changes without causal claims about MiniMax internals.

methodology.title: Reliability Operationalization
methodology.detail: LLM-as-judge reliability is decomposed into four constructs: judgment validity (accuracy, Cohen’s κ, Spearman correlation), bias robustness (position flip, verbosity bias, granularity sensitivity), aggregation independence (error correlation ρ, jury gain), and protocol auditability (parse status, fallback behavior, intermediate verdicts).

methodology.title: Datasets and Judges
methodology.detail: Eight judges (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 14B, 32B; MiniMax M2, M2.1, M2.5, M2.7) are evaluated on four datasets: LLMBar (419 adversarial pairs), PandaLM testset-v1 (894 pairwise examples), Chatbot Arena seed-42 (1,997 pairwise examples), and Judge’s Verdict (200 TechQA-derived examples with pointwise labels).

methodology.title: Aggregation and Debate Protocols
methodology.detail: Jury aggregation experiments estimate intra-class error correlation ρ to assess independence assumptions. Debate experiments analyze decision shifts but highlight the need for parser and fallback logs to attribute changes to deliberation.

mechanism.title: Evaluator-Replacement Ambiguity
mechanism.detail: The paper conceptualizes the measurement pipeline as comprising candidate responses, benchmark slice, judge model, prompt/decoding, parser, and aggregation/debate. Changes in any component, especially the judge model, can alter reported scores, creating ambiguity about the source of score changes.

mechanism.title: Error Correlation and Jury Aggregation
mechanism.detail: High intra-class error correlation ρ among jurors violates independence assumptions of Condorcet-style majority voting, limiting jury accuracy gains. The beta-binomial model corrected by ρ accurately predicts jury accuracy, showing that correlated errors constrain aggregation benefits.

experiments.title: Judge Upgrade Evaluation
experiments.detail: Evaluated eight judges across four datasets using fixed main prompts. Metrics include accuracy, Cohen’s κ, and Spearman correlation. The study compares adjacent judge upgrades along parameter scaling and released-model axes to assess reliability gains.

experiments.title: Bias Probing
experiments.detail: Position-flip rates, verbosity bias, and granularity sensitivity are measured to assess bias robustness. Results show stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate these biases, with position-flip rates decreasing from 0.320 (Qwen3-1.7B) to 0.117–0.147 (MiniMax releases).

experiments.title: Jury Aggregation Experiment
experiments.detail: Homogeneous and heterogeneous juries are formed to test aggregation gains. Error correlation ρ is estimated from vote matrices, showing high correlation (up to 0.972) that limits majority voting improvements. Beta-binomial models corrected by ρ closely predict observed jury accuracy.

experiments.title: Debate Protocol Case Study
experiments.detail: Structured debate experiments reveal substantial decision shifts, but lack of parser and fallback logs prevents attribution of these shifts to deliberation, highlighting the need for audit trails in debate protocols.

findings.title: Non-Interchangeability of Judge Upgrades
findings.detail: Only Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters yields a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability; MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not show consistent improvements across datasets.

findings.title: Bias Reduction but Persistence
findings.detail: Stronger judges reduce position-flip rates from 0.320 to approximately 0.117–0.147 and verbosity bias from 0.547 to about 0.13, but biases remain nonzero, indicating capability improves but does not eliminate bias.

findings.title: Limited Jury Gains Due to Correlated Errors
findings.detail: High intra-class error correlations (ρ = 0.944–0.972 for Qwen3 juries) cause majority voting to yield minimal accuracy improvements, with jury size increases from 1 to 5 only marginally improving accuracy (e.g., 0.463 to 0.482 on LLMBar).

findings.title: Debate Shifts Require Audit Trails
findings.detail: Structured debate can substantially change decisions, but without parser and fallback logs, these shifts cannot be confidently attributed to deliberation processes.

findings.title: Dataset-Specific Evaluator Strength
findings.detail: No single judge dominates all datasets: GLM-5.1 leads on LLMBar, MiniMax-M2.7 leads on PandaLM, and mimo-v2-pro leads on Chatbot Arena, emphasizing slice-specific measurement validity.

contributions: Formulation of evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem in LLM-as-judge evaluation.
A two-axis empirical study comparing parameter scaling and released-model upgrades across multiple datasets and judges.
Decomposition of LLM-as-judge reliability into judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability.
Demonstration that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases and that jury aggregation gains are limited by correlated errors.
Proposal of a reporting standard including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.
limitations: No causal claims are made about MiniMax internal model changes due to lack of controlled ablation.
Absence of parser and fallback logs limits attribution of debate-induced decision shifts to actual deliberation.
Bias and reliability analyses are limited to the evaluated datasets and judge panels, restricting generalizability.
Prompt sensitivity is treated as a robustness check but not systematically explored, leaving prompt effects under-specified.
open_questions: How can audit trails be designed to reliably attribute decision shifts in multi-agent debate protocols?
What mechanisms underlie the persistence of bias despite increased evaluator capability?
Can error correlation among heterogeneous juries be reduced to improve aggregation gains?
How do prompt variations interact with evaluator scaling to affect measurement validity?
